text: Question two. How does an incremental model actually filter new rows? With a watermark: the latest timestamp already loaded. On an incremental run, a guard adds one condition to the model: only source rows newer than the maximum in the model's own table. On the page's tables, the model holds events through January fourteenth, and the source has twenty-four. The filter loads the ten after the watermark. Then three more land. Event twenty-five has the same timestamp as the new watermark. Twenty-six happened on the twenty-second and arrived late. Twenty-seven is simply new. A strict greater-than finds only twenty-seven. The other two are never loaded, and nothing errors. Greater-than-or-equal, plus deduplication, catches the tie: twenty-five comes in, and twenty-four, read again, is skipped. But twenty-six is older than the watermark, so it's still missed. So production models re-read an overlap window, here the last three days, and merge on a stable key. The window reads seven rows, and all three new ones land. Make the window as wide as your data arrives late. A wider one re-reads more on every run, and an event later than the window still slips past. The other way out is a change sequence the source guarantees only ever grows, so nothing can land behind the watermark. Question three. What is the "this" variable in dbt? It's the model's own table in the warehouse, the one the filter takes its maximum from. On the very first run that table doesn't exist yet, so the incremental check returns false, the guard is skipped, and the model loads everything.
